families.title: Octagon streets
families.mathematics: A robot walks the roads of a floor: each move turns left, goes straight on or turns right at a dot and walks one road. On the octagon floor every room is an octagon with right-angled corners and four rooms meet at every dot, the {8,4} tiling of the hyperbolic plane, drawn in the Poincaré disk and recentred on the robot; beside it is the square floor, the {4,4} tiling. The robot’s place and heading is an element of the rotation group ⟨T, H | T⁴ = H² = (TH)^p = 1⟩ (p = 8 or 4), kept as its word and reduced by a complete rewriting system, so returns are exact. Facts: on octagons the shortest walk home facing the same way is 8 moves (round a room), then 14 (round two rooms); 4 and 6 are impossible, because the roads have girth 8 and a walk of up to three roads is the only short route between its ends; every odd length is impossible on both floors, because every road joins a light dot to a dark one. A fence (a closed walk using no dot twice) round n rooms has left minus right turns 4 + 4n on octagons and 4 on squares (Gauss–Bonnet: the turning is a full turn plus the area inside, and an octagon here has area 2π), so two octagons need 12 left turns: 16 corners less the 4 at the ends of their shared wall.
rules: Each move turns left, goes straight on or turns right at a dot, then walks one road. The robot never turns round.

On the octagon floor every room has eight corners, all right angles, and four rooms meet at every dot. The floor slides so the robot stays in the middle; rooms near the rim are drawn smaller but are all the same size.
Can’t works once a try is finished. When Can’t is not right, it waits for a different finished try.

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts where the robot will end up before each move, and which floor surprises them.
parent.prompt: Make the same moves on both floors. When do they end up in the same kind of place?
parent.explanation: On squares a turn left and three turns right come to the same heading, and four left moves close a loop. On octagons four left moves go only halfway round a room, and two different short routes never end at the same dot: the smallest loop is eight roads.
parent.extension: Find a walk that comes home facing the same way on both floors. (Eight lefts does: twice round a square, once round an octagon.)
parent.connection: The two floors are the {4,4} tiling of the flat plane and the {8,4} tiling of the hyperbolic plane; their rotation groups have the same generators and differ in one relation.

parent.notice: Whether your child expects four left turns to make a loop, as on squares, and what they do when it doesn’t.
parent.prompt: Where did four left turns take the robot? How many more did it need?
parent.explanation: Every room is an octagon whose corners are right angles, and four rooms meet at each dot. Four left turns take the robot halfway round one room; it is home facing the same way after eight, one for each corner. Of all 3^8 = 6,561 walks of eight moves, only eight lefts and eight rights come home facing the same way.
parent.extension: Can the robot come home in fewer than eight moves? (No: Puzzles 2 and 4 show why not in four or six.)
parent.connection: The floor is the {8,4} tiling of the hyperbolic plane. Gauss–Bonnet: the turning round a loop is a full turn plus the area inside, measured as an angle. A room here has area 2π, so going round one takes two full turns, eight quarter turns.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries four lefts on the octagons, sees it stop halfway round a room, and looks for a way to say why no other walk works either.
parent.prompt: After two moves, how many ways are there back home in two roads?
parent.explanation: On squares, four lefts or four rights come home facing the same way (2 of the 81 walks). On octagons none of the 81 walks does. After two moves the robot is two roads from home. Two different two-road routes between the same dots would close up a loop of four roads, but the smallest loop on this floor goes round a room of eight. So the only two-road way back is the way it came, and that starts with a turn round, which no move allows. The dot after two moves is the certificate the child taps.
parent.extension: Does the same argument work for six moves? (Yes, with the dot after three moves: Puzzle 4.)
parent.connection: The roads form a graph of girth 8 (shortest cycle 8), so any route of up to three roads is the only shortest route between its ends.

parent.notice: Whether your child counts the left turns on each floor, and what they make of 12 against 4.
parent.prompt: Two rooms on each floor. Why does one fence need so many more left turns?
parent.explanation: The tightest fences are straight, left, left, straight, left, left on squares (4 lefts) and straight, six lefts, straight, six lefts on octagons (12 lefts). Two octagons have 16 corners; at the two ends of their shared wall the fence goes straight on, and the 4 corners there are lost, leaving 12 left turns. Two squares have 8 corners and lose 4, leaving 4. Within 30 moves there are 455 fences on squares (every rectangle with home on its bottom edge) and 123 on octagons.
parent.extension: Fence three flowers in a row on each floor. (Octagons 16 lefts, squares still 4.)
parent.connection: Round n rooms, left turns minus right turns is 4 + 4n on octagons and always 4 on squares (Gauss–Bonnet).

parent.notice: Whether your child reuses Puzzle 2’s reason with three moves in place of two.
parent.prompt: Which dot would the robot have to turn round at?
parent.explanation: On squares six walks of the 729 come home facing the same way: round a block of two squares, turning left all the way or right all the way, with home at one of three places on the way round (left, left, straight, left, left, straight is one). On octagons none does: after three moves the robot is three roads from home, and two different routes of three roads would make a loop of six, but the smallest loop is eight. So the only three-road way back is the way it came, starting with a turn round.
parent.extension: What about ten or twelve moves? (Also impossible on octagons, but the halfway reason no longer works, because routes of four roads can differ, round half a room. Fourteen works: Puzzle 7.)
parent.connection: Returns on the {8,4} floor happen at lengths 8, 14, 16, 18, 20, …: 2, 14, 50, 144 and 620 walks.

parent.notice: Whether your child notices that this one fails on both floors, unlike four and six.
parent.prompt: If every road joins a light dot to a dark one, what colour is the robot on after one move? After two? After seven?
parent.explanation: Colour the dots so every road joins a light dot to a dark one; both floors can be coloured like a chessboard. Home is light, and every move walks one road, so the colour changes at every move. After seven moves the robot is on a dark dot, never home. After Can’t the child taps the dots of the walk that share home’s colour, the ones it reached after two, four and six moves (other than home), and the app then draws the whole colouring. Those dots show the colours alternating along the walk, which puts the seventh dot on the other colour.
parent.extension: Does the colouring also rule out 13 moves? (Yes: Puzzle 10.)
parent.connection: Both floors are bipartite graphs, because every room has an even number of sides.

parent.notice: Whether your child first tries to fence just the two flowers, and finds the fence would have to use the corner dot twice.
parent.prompt: What happens at the dot where the two flowers meet?
parent.explanation: A fence never uses a dot twice, so where the flowers meet, a third room must be inside too. That room leaves the fourth room at the dot outside, and the fence would bend in round it: a right turn. So with no right turns all four rooms at the dot are inside. Their fence is 24 moves: straight, five lefts, four times, with 20 left turns, 4 + 4 × 4. There are 17 fences within 30 moves; the others take in a fifth room.
parent.extension: Puzzle 9 allows a right turn. How few left turns can a fence round both flowers have then?
parent.connection: Round n rooms, left minus right turns is 4 + 4n; here n = 4.

parent.notice: Whether your child thinks of leaving a room out, and accepts the right turn that this needs at the corner dot.
parent.prompt: Puzzle 6 took 20 left turns. Why does leaving out one room save three of them?
parent.explanation: A fence must take a third room at the dot where the flowers meet, so it goes round three rooms with the fourth room at that dot outside, turning right there. Three rooms have 24 corners. The fence is 20 roads long: it goes straight at the outer ends of the two shared walls, turns right at the middle dot, and turns left at the other 17 corners: 17 − 1 = 16 = 4 + 4 × 3. There are exactly two such fences (leave out either of the two other rooms), and none with 19 lefts or fewer round four rooms (20 lefts).
parent.extension: On squares, an L of three squares takes 5 lefts and 1 right. Why only 4 + 0 × 3 there?

puzzles.title: Thirteen moves home
puzzles.objective: Come home facing the same way in exactly 13 moves on this floor, or press Can’t where no walk can.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Home in exactly 13 moves, facing the same way.
puzzles.instruction: Come home facing the same way in exactly 13 moves on this floor, or press Can’t where no walk can.
puzzles.controls: A move turns at a dot (left, straight on or right) and then walks one road to the next dot; the robot never turns round. Home facing the same way means back on the yellow ring, pointing like the faint arrow. Tap ↰, ↑ or ↱, or a road ahead of the robot. Drag a floor to look round it. After a try, if no walk can do it, press Can’t and tap the dots that show why.
rules: Each move turns left, goes straight on or turns right at a dot, then walks one road. The robot never turns round.

On the octagon floor every room has eight corners, all right angles, and four rooms meet at every dot. The floor slides so the robot stays in the middle; rooms near the rim are drawn smaller but are all the same size.
Make exactly 13 moves. The walk must end on the yellow ring with the robot pointing like the faint arrow.
Can’t works once a try is finished. When Can’t is not right, it waits for a different finished try.
puzzles.idea: Thirteen is one short of fourteen, and no odd walk comes home.
puzzles.prerequisites: Tell left from right and count moves. The reason for Can’t is a colouring idea a grown-up can draw on paper first.
hints: Fourteen moves worked in Puzzle 7. Try thirteen.
Colour the dots light and dark so every road joins two colours. What colour is the robot on after thirteen moves?
After thirteen moves, press Can’t and tap every dot your walk reached after an even number of moves, other than home.

parent.notice: Whether your child reaches for Puzzle 5’s colouring rather than trying many walks.
parent.prompt: Is there any odd number of moves that works?
parent.explanation: Every move changes the colour of the robot’s dot, so after thirteen moves it is on a dark dot and home is light. None of the 1,594,323 walks of thirteen moves comes home. After Can’t the child taps the walk’s dots of home’s colour (those reached after an even number of moves, other than home), and the app draws the colouring.
parent.extension: On the octagon floor, which even numbers of moves can come home? (8 and every even number from 14 on; not 2, 4, 6, 10 or 12.)
parent.connection: The floor is bipartite because every room has eight sides, an even number.
